job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup we want to send Senator Whitfield's office a list of fixes. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let mining companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — Per-vessel threshold.** The definition only covers recovery above 10,000 metric tons per year by a *single vessel*. Operators could stay below the threshold or split production across vessels, companies, or affiliated operators; it also leaves unclear how the yearly limit is measured and whether it applies per site or across operations.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Unclear scope of “mineral resources.”** The text does not specify whether the term includes all seabed minerals, processing or handling recovered material, or only the listed nodules and “other mineral resources.” That uncertainty could let operators argue that particular resources or parts of an operation fall outside the definition.

3. **Section 2(1)(B) — Discretionary risk test.** Whether an activity is covered depends on a Secretary’s determination, with no criteria, deadline, or process for making it. Companies could argue that an activity is not prohibited until such a determination is made, and the open-ended standard invites inconsistent application or challenge.

4. **Section 2(2) — Narrow “U.S. person” definition.** It omits U.S. residents, partnerships, other business entities, and potentially corporations organized outside the United States but controlled by U.S. persons. Those actors could contend they are not subject to the prohibition when operating abroad.

5. **Section 2(3) — Narrow “covered vessel” definition.** The 5,000-gross-ton threshold and vessel-based definition omit smaller vessels, support ships, and potentially remotely operated systems. Since registration and reporting apply only to covered vessels, operators could avoid those obligations by using other equipment or dividing operations.

6. **Section 3(a) — Unclear reach and covered conduct.** “Any person in the United States” does not say whether it covers U.S. territory, waters, ports, or conduct such as financing, brokering, transporting, processing, or importing mined minerals. The provision also prohibits only activity meeting the narrow definition of commercial mining, leaving other stages or participants open to arguments that they are outside the ban.

7. **Section 3(b) — Existing-operations exception.** The exception has no end date, phase-out, limits on locations or activities, or requirement that the license remain valid. It could be read to authorize ongoing mining under any pre-enactment exploration license, even if operations expand or the license is later transferred or renewed.

8. **Section 3(c) — Environmental-assessment exception.** “For the purpose of environmental assessment” is undefined and has no limits, safeguards, or independent approval requirement. An operator could characterize mineral recovery as assessment-related, potentially allowing substantial extraction under the exception.

9. **Section 4(a) — Registration is incomplete.** There is no deadline, required information, renewal process, or consequence for failing to register, and the duty applies only to covered vessels. This makes the registry difficult to use to identify and monitor operations and invites disputes over compliance.

10. **Section 4(b) — Reports do not track the ban.** Reports describe recovery activities but need not identify locations, quantities, customers, ownership, or other relevant conduct; there is no deadline for filing, public-access rule, or verification mechanism. Operators outside the registry can avoid reporting altogether, and the provision does not expressly make false or missing reports a separate violation.

11. **Section 5(a) — Civil penalty may be inadequate or uncertain.** The maximum is discretionary, with no minimum or factors for setting it, and “each day” does not clarify how continuing or multiple violations are counted. The section also does not specify which agency may assess penalties or provide an enforcement process, complicating collection and consistent deterrence.

12. **Section 5(b) — Criminal penalty lacks clear enforcement provisions.** The provision does not identify who investigates or prosecutes violations, and “willfully” may be difficult to prove without clarification of the required knowledge or intent. It also does not state how penalties apply to responsible officers or other individuals acting for an entity.

13. **Section 6 — No obligation to achieve an agreement.** The Secretary need only “seek to negotiate,” with no required outcome, reporting, or interim measures. The 18-month deadline could be met by minimal efforts, while the section does not itself prevent foreign operators from mining.

14. **Section 7(a) — Unworkable duration condition.** It is unclear what report Congress must act on, what “serious harm” means, or whether the joint resolution must be enacted into law. The provision also does not explain how a prohibition can remain in effect until Congress acts when Section 7(b) separately ends the Act after ten years.

15. **Section 7(b) — Automatic sunset defeats the prohibition.** The Act expires after ten years regardless of whether Congress has found mining safe or an international agreement has been reached. The sunset could allow mining to resume without any affirmative safety finding.

16. **Section 8 — Delayed effective date creates a gap.** The Act does not take effect for 180 days, leaving a period in which the prohibition and its penalties do not apply. The bill does not restrict new licenses or operations during that period, and the interaction between this delay and the “date of enactment” exceptions and penalty language is unclear.
